text:
Evidence supports recency-aware training as a plausible improvement, but does not establish that positional loss weights specifically reduce stale-interest recommendations. [Petrov & Macdonald (RecSys 2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.02643) introduce recency-biased positive sampling and report effectiveness improvements across GRU4Rec, Caser and SASRec. This changes training-target sampling, rather than simply weighting ordinary next-item losses. [Li et al. (2024)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0952197624015240) more directly investigate time-aware loss weighting, including learned weights. Neither result alone demonstrates reduced preference staleness.

[LinkedIn’s Feed SR report](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.12354v1) explicitly distinguishes positional loss decay within histories from timestamp-based sample weighting. It provides a practical precedent, although its transformer feed-ranking setting differs from GRU4Rec on Amazon. Position measures interaction order; elapsed time measures actual age. Training weights influence parameter learning, whereas inference decay changes how history contributes to current predictions. Excessive recency emphasis can also hurt: [Oh & Cho (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.09722) document recency bias and impaired ranking performance. Their last-item recommendation metric is unsuitable after unseen-item filtering removes that item.

Recommended ablations: uniform versus positional-weighted next-item loss; positional versus timestamp weighting; training weighting alone versus a jointly trained, time-decayed history representation alone versus both. Retain one GRU network per category, normalize weights over nonpadding targets, and match training budgets, negatives, seeds and checkpoint selection. Sweep decay strength, including zero. Select using the fixed macro validation HR@10; inspect per-category results and timestamp-gap/history-length strata. Treat reduced staleness as a hypothesis: HR@10 gains alone do not establish that mechanism.
